steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for a paper on measuring cultural bias in language models in Arabic, i.e. whether LMs favour Western entities over Arab ones, and the benchmark we built to test it.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Why multicultural LMs matter
- Motivating example: Western-centric completions in Arabic
- Gap in bias research and the CAMeL benchmark
- Experiments and results
- Analysis of pre-training corpora

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Multicultural LMs
  - multicultural world; LMs deployed globally -> must grasp cultural distinctions
  - progress on language barrier, but LMs still miss cultural nuances / context
  - truly multicultural LMs: across languages + cultural sensitivity
- Example (Figure 1)
  - Arabic prompts -> Western-centric completions
  - alcoholic beverages even when prompt mentions Islamic prayer
  - "going for a drink": alcohol in the West vs coffee or tea in predominantly Muslim Arab world
  - Western names, food dishes too
  - users may be upset; question: do LMs exhibit bias towards Western entities in non-English, non-Western languages?
- Gap + CAMeL
  - bias studied across demographic/social groups: religion, race, nationalities
  - little work (§ 2) on cultural appropriateness in non-Western, non-English settings
  - focus on culturally relevant entities: cultural heritage, regional identities
  - no existing resource contrasting Arab vs Western
  - CAMeL (Cultural Appropriateness Measure Set for LMs): 20,368 Arab and Western entities from Wikidata and CommonCrawl
  - eight types: person names, food dishes, beverages, clothing items, locations, authors, religious places of worship, sports clubs
  - 628 naturally occurring prompts (§ 3)
- Experiments (§ 4)
  - story generation, NER, sentiment analysis, text infilling
  - 16 LMs pre-trained with Arabic data (§ 4.1)
  - stereotypes in stories: Arab names with poverty/traditionalism (§ 4.2)
  - unfairness: better NER on Western entities, Arab entities more negative sentiment (§ 4.3)
  - preference for Western entities even in contexts suited to Arab ones (§ 4.4)
- Corpora (§ 5)
  - Western content in Arabic corpora as key contributor
  - 6 Arabic pre-training corpora, n-gram LMs, text-infilling on CAMeL
  - Wikipedia may not be ideal for culturally-aware LMs

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
We live in a multicultural world, and the diversity of cultures enriches our global community. Since LMs are deployed globally, it is very important to make sure these models understand the cultural distinctions of different communities. There has been progress in bridging the language barrier gap, but LMs still struggle to capture cultural nuances and to adapt to specific cultural contexts. Truly multicultural LMs should not only communicate across languages but also be aware of cultural sensitivities when they do so, which fosters a deeper global connection.

As Figure 1 shows, LMs fail to adapt appropriately to culture in Arabic when they are asked to complete various prompts, and they often suggest and prioritize Western-centric content. For example, LMs mention alcoholic beverages even when the Arabic prompt explicitly mentions Islamic prayer. In Western culture "going for a drink" commonly means drinking alcoholic beverages, but in the predominantly Muslim Arab world, where alcohol is not prevalent, the same phrase in everyday life often means drinking coffee or tea. LMs also generate Western-centric entities when they suggest people's names and food dishes, even though these are not appropriate to the cultural context of the prompts. These observations are concerning, because users may be upset to see inadequate cultural representation by LMs in their own languages. So this leads to the question: do LMs exhibit bias towards Western entities in non-English, non-Western languages?

A lot of effort has gone into exploring biases in LMs with regard to groups of different demographic or social dimensions, such as religion, race, and nationalities, but much less work (§ 2) has looked at whether LMs are culturally appropriate in non-Western and non-English environments. To address this gap, our study centers on culturally relevant entities, because they are important parts of cultural heritage and can symbolize regional identities. As far as we know there is no resource readily available for this, especially one that contrasts Arab vs. Western cultural differences. So we construct a new benchmark, CAMeL (Cultural Appropriateness Measure Set for LMs). It consists of an extensive list of 20,368 Arab and Western entities extracted from Wikidata and CommonCrawl, covering eight entity types (person names, food dishes, beverages, clothing items, locations, authors, religious places of worship, and sports clubs), and an associated set of 628 naturally occurring prompts that serve as contexts for those entities (§ 3).

- Experiments (§ 4)
  - story generation, NER, sentiment analysis, text infilling; 16 LMs pre-trained with Arabic data (§ 4.1)
  - stereotypes: Arab names with poverty/traditionalism (§ 4.2)
  - unfairness: better NER on Western entities, Arab entities more negative sentiment (§ 4.3)
  - preference for Western entities even in Arab-suited contexts (§ 4.4)
- Corpora (§ 5)
  - Western content in Arabic corpora as possible cause; 6 corpora, n-gram LMs, text infilling on CAMeL
  - Wikipedia may not be ideal

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
We live in a multicultural world, and the diversity of cultures enriches our global community. Since LMs are deployed globally, it is very important to make sure these models understand the cultural distinctions of different communities. There has been progress in bridging the language barrier gap, but LMs still struggle to capture cultural nuances and to adapt to specific cultural contexts. Truly multicultural LMs should not only communicate across languages but also be aware of cultural sensitivities when they do so, which fosters a deeper global connection.

As Figure 1 shows, LMs fail to adapt appropriately to culture in Arabic when they are asked to complete various prompts, and they often suggest and prioritize Western-centric content. For example, LMs mention alcoholic beverages even when the Arabic prompt explicitly mentions Islamic prayer. In Western culture "going for a drink" commonly means drinking alcoholic beverages, but in the predominantly Muslim Arab world, where alcohol is not prevalent, the same phrase in everyday life often means drinking coffee or tea. LMs also generate Western-centric entities when they suggest people's names and food dishes, even though these are not appropriate to the cultural context of the prompts. These observations are concerning, because users may be upset to see inadequate cultural representation by LMs in their own languages. So this leads to the question: do LMs exhibit bias towards Western entities in non-English, non-Western languages?

A lot of effort has gone into exploring biases in LMs with regard to groups of different demographic or social dimensions, such as religion, race, and nationalities, but much less work (§ 2) has looked at whether LMs are culturally appropriate in non-Western and non-English environments. To address this gap, our study centers on culturally relevant entities, because they are important parts of cultural heritage and can symbolize regional identities. As far as we know there is no resource readily available for this, especially one that contrasts Arab vs. Western cultural differences. So we construct a new benchmark, CAMeL (Cultural Appropriateness Measure Set for LMs). It consists of an extensive list of 20,368 Arab and Western entities extracted from Wikidata and CommonCrawl, covering eight entity types (person names, food dishes, beverages, clothing items, locations, authors, religious places of worship, and sports clubs), and an associated set of 628 naturally occurring prompts that serve as contexts for those entities (§ 3).

We show that CAMeL entities and prompts make it possible to test LMs cross-culturally in different experimental setups, including story generation, NER, sentiment analysis, and text infilling (§ 4). We benchmark 16 LMs that were pre-trained with Arabic data (§ 4.1). The results show concerning cases of cultural stereotypes in stories generated by LMs, such as Arab names being associated with poverty/traditionalism (§ 4.2), and cultural unfairness, such as NER tagging working better on Western entities and Arab entities being more associated with negative sentiment (§ 4.3). We also show that LMs have high levels of preference for Western-associated entities, even when the prompts are contexts uniquely suited for entities associated with Arab culture (§ 4.4).

Finally, we discuss that the prevalence of Western content in Arabic corpora may be a key contributor to the biases we observe in LMs. We analyze how culturally relevant 6 Arabic pre-training corpora are by training n-gram LMs on each corpus and comparing how they do at text infilling on CAMeL. We find that sources like Wikipedia may not be ideal for building culturally-aware LMs (§ 5).

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
We live in a multicultural world, where the diversity of cultures enriches our global community. Given the global deployment of LMs, it is crucial to ensure these models grasp the cultural distinctions of diverse communities. Despite progress in bridging the language barrier gap [1,2], LMs still struggle at capturing cultural nuances and adapting to specific cultural contexts [3]. Truly multicultural LMs should not only communicate across languages but do so with an awareness of cultural sensitivities, fostering a deeper global connection.

As we show in Figure 1, LMs fail at appropriate cultural adaptation in Arabic when asked to complete various prompts, often suggesting and prioritizing Western-centric content. For example, LMs refer to alcoholic beverages even when the prompt in Arabic explicitly mentions Islamic prayer. While "going for a drink" in Western culture commonly refers to consuming alcoholic beverages, in the predominantly Muslim Arab world, where alcohol is not prevalent, the same phrase in everyday life often refers to drinking coffee or tea. LMs also generate Western-centric entities when suggesting people's names and food dishes, despite these being inappropriate to the cultural context of the prompts. Such observations raise concerns, as users may find it upsetting to see inadequate cultural representation by LMs in their own languages. This leads to the question: do LMs exhibit bias towards Western entities in non-English, non-Western languages?

While considerable effort has gone into exploring biases in LMs with regard to groups of different demographic or social dimensions [4] such as religion [5,6], race [7,8], and nationalities [9], much less work (§ 2) has examined the cultural appropriateness of LMs in non-Western and non-English environments. To address this gap, we center our study on culturally relevant entities, as they are important aspects of cultural heritage [10,11] and can symbolize regional identities [12]. To the best of our knowledge, no resource is readily available for doing so, especially one that contrasts Arab vs. Western cultural differences. We therefore construct a new benchmark, CAMeL (Cultural Appropriateness Measure Set for LMs), which consists of an extensive list of 20,368 Arab and Western entities extracted from Wikidata and CommonCrawl, covering eight entity types (i.e., person names, food dishes, beverages, clothing items, locations, authors, religious places of worship, and sports clubs), and an associated set of 628 naturally occurring prompts as contexts for those entities (§ 3).

We show that CAMeL entities and prompts enable cross-cultural testing of LMs in versatile experimental setups, including story generation, NER, sentiment analysis, and text infilling (§ 4). We benchmark 16 LMs pre-trained with Arabic data (§ 4.1). Our results reveal concerning cases of cultural stereotypes in LM-generated stories, such as the association of Arab names with poverty/traditionalism (§ 4.2), and cultural unfairness, such as better NER tagging performance on Western entities and a higher association of Arab entities with negative sentiment (§ 4.3). We further show that LMs exhibit high levels of preference towards Western-associated entities even when prompted by contexts uniquely suited for Arab culture-associated entities (§ 4.4).

Lastly, we discuss how the prevalence of Western content in Arabic corpora may be a key contributor to the biases observed in LMs. We analyze the cultural relevance of 6 Arabic pre-training corpora by training n-gram LMs on each corpus and comparing their text-infilling performance on CAMeL. We find that sources such as Wikipedia may not be ideal for building culturally-aware LMs (§ 5).
